claims.text: The damaged component is a nickel-based superalloy turbine blade.
The blade has existing microstructural degradation.
The blade material is susceptible to hot cracking during conventional fusion welding.
Localized friction stir repair processing is proposed for the damaged area.
Optimized tool rotation and traverse speeds can maintain the local processing temperature below 0.6 Tm.
The friction stir repair is to be performed under an inert atmosphere.
Temperatures of 700–900 degrees Celsius and high-stress fatigue loading are representative of aggressive turbine-engine operation.
Friction stir repair will produce a dynamically recrystallized, fine-grained repair zone.
The repair zone will contain minimal unmixed or defective regions.
Severe plastic deformation from the rotating tool induces dynamic recrystallization.
Dynamic recrystallization results in a uniformly consolidated repair zone.
Avoiding full melting suppresses the liquid-phase formation associated with hot cracking.
The friction stir repaired zone will have greater toughness than a conventional fusion-welded repair.
The friction stir repaired zone will have greater fatigue resistance than a conventional fusion-welded repair.
The friction stir repaired zone will be more resistant to hot cracking than a conventional fusion-welded repair.
Full melting and rapid cooling during traditional fusion welding of nickel-based superalloys promote hot cracking and inferior microstructural continuity.
Incomplete recrystallization and unmixed zones may occur if tool geometry and processing parameters are not optimized.
